overview: This file consists of an August 8, 1947 Department of State memorandum recording an interdepartmental conversation about the price the United States should pay for stocks of tin found in postwar Japan that had been looted from Malaya and the Netherlands East Indies. It documents disagreement over whether the tin should be valued at the lower U.S. buying price in Malaya or at the U.S. selling price prevailing for international allocations, in light of an informal 1946 Anglo-American understanding that none of the recovered material would be sold as “cheap tin.”

people.name: Virginia D. Karchere
people.role: Department of State participant and author of the memorandum

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on the Price of Looted Tin Found in Japan
subfiles.from: Virginia D. Karchere, Department of State
subfiles.about: Records Marion Worthing’s reservations about using the U.S. buying price in Malaya to value tin looted from Malaya and the Netherlands East Indies and later recovered in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Marion Worthing recalled an informal 1946 understanding between the British and the United States that recovered tin would not be sold below prevailing market prices. She argued that the United States should therefore pay its selling price rather than its lower buying price in Malaya, particularly because the United States was now expected to purchase almost all the tin. Worthing noted that the buying price used for 1946 should also have been reconsidered in light of the earlier understanding and formally stated her reservations about the current U.S. position.

interest: The memorandum offers a compact view of the practical disputes surrounding the disposal and restitution of resources looted by Japan during the war. It is especially useful for showing how informal wartime or early postwar understandings influenced later commodity-pricing policy, and how U.S. agencies could differ over whether recovered goods should be acquired cheaply or sold on terms consistent with international allocation prices. The expectation that the United States would buy nearly all the tin also illuminates American influence in postwar raw-material markets.
